chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.html:
“My house is assessed at such-and-such by the city.” You hear that sentence often — and it leads to plenty of misunderstandings about pricing. The municipal assessment and market value are two different things, with two distinct uses.

This guide clarifies the difference, explains the comparative factor, and helps you use the right figure at the right time.

Each chapter ends with a lined “My Notes” page.

chapters.title: The Municipal Assessment: A Tax Tool
chapters.html:
Understanding what it's really for.

The municipal assessment appears on the assessment roll. It's used to allocate municipal and school taxes. It's established in bulk, as of a reference date, for an entire territory — not property by property at the current price.

It can therefore be higher or lower than the actual market value, and often with a time lag.

Emilie's tip

The municipal assessment answers one question: “how much tax do I pay?” It does not answer “what is my house worth on the market today?” Never confuse the two.

chapters.title: Market Value: The Market Price
chapters.objective: Understanding what a buyer actually pays.
chapters.html:
Understanding what a buyer actually pays.

Market value is the price an informed buyer is willing to pay today, under current conditions. It's determined by a comparative market analysis (recent similar sales), not by the assessment roll.

It's this figure — and this figure alone — that should guide a listing price or a purchase offer.

Emilie's tip

To buy or sell, rely on market value (a comparative analysis), never on the municipal assessment. The market doesn't consult the assessment roll to decide what to pay.

chapters.title: The Comparative Factor and Proper Uses
chapters.html:
Connecting the two concepts correctly.

The municipality applies a “comparative factor” to try to bring the assessment roll closer to market value (for example, to calculate the Welcome Tax). This clearly shows that the assessment, on its own, is not the market value.

  • Municipal assessment: for taxes, and as the (adjusted) basis for the Welcome Tax.
  • Market value: to set a listing price or an offer.
  • Never negotiate a price based solely on the municipal assessment.
Emilie's tip

If a seller or buyer cites the “municipal assessment” to justify a price, bring the discussion back to comparables. That's the only solid ground for agreeing on a value.

chapters.title: Action Plan
chapters.html:
Your next steps, in concrete terms.

This week

  1. Find my municipal assessment and its date.
  2. Request a comparative analysis for the market value.

Within 30 days

  1. Use market value for any pricing decision.
  2. Understand the comparative factor for the Welcome Tax.

After that

  1. Stop confusing the two figures.

chapters.title: Resources & Glossary
chapters.html:
• Assessment roll: the municipal register of values, the basis for taxes.
  • Municipal assessment: a tax value, distinct from the sale price.
  • Market value: the price an informed buyer pays today.
  • Comparative factor: a coefficient bringing the assessment closer to the market.
  • Comparative analysis: recent sales used to determine market value.
